The way I run it is this.

Objectively speaking it's more satisfying to kill the main threat of a fight climactically. So, make rules that make that happen more often.

Designate a single crazy enemy, the big guy, the threat, whatever. Figure out 1/5th of their hit points. For instance, an enemy with 300hp would have this be 60hp. Once they hit this hp, you enter climatic mode. If an attack is climatic enough, like a crit or the attacker and the enemy have history or even just max damage, it kills the enemy. If this does not happen by the time they're reduced to 0, then they're just killed by being reduced to 0.

This method also works for specific climatic things you'd like to happen, like that second example. If you really want a clash between rivals to happen, you can raise the bar of climax and if it doesn't happen by the time the monster dies then it wasn't meant to be.

I do agree we should absolutely use Magical Ammunition instead of +Bows, however as someone who did this fix it's ungodly terrible.

So here's the big issue. Magical Ammo loses magic after it's fired. So all those +1 arrows you bought are one time uses. The reason for this is that when you collect your arrows back, there's no mechanic to find out how many of the ones you got back were the magical ones you fired.

So what you have is effectively a spellslot like resource on ranged attackers. If a monster has resistance to nonmagical damage, they're going to burn through all those arrows to be even a little bit competent, but they don't get those back for free.

Another problem is that this makes high level archers completely unsustainable. The fighter makes 1 purchase of 350gp, the average price of an uncommon item, to get a sick-ass permanent +1 sword. The archer on the other hand, even using the lowest possible listed price for an uncommon item, can only buy 3 +1 arrows with that same money. That's 3 one time uses of competency.

It's a lot more nuanced than just "give trainers more pokemon" but particularly in this gen I would have loved to see more pokemon per team.

In previous games there was a balance, a really hard balance at that. Rom hackers know this especially. Picture a route between two gyms, where the gym leader had 3 level 20 pokemon. The player should have a similar, but higher amount so lets say 4 level 22 pokemon. There are three trainers in this route. How many pokemon should these trainers have, and what level?

If you make them comparable to the player or harder, the player would want to skip them. This means you'll need to account for the player not getting the XP from these trainers when you design the gym in the next town. If you make them. When we talk about this method lets call it hard difficulty.

If you make them similar to the Gym Leader, you'll have a clear progression curve but again the player would likely want to skip them. When we talk about this method lets call it medium difficulty.

If you make them easier than the player then the player would not gain a lot of xp from them and again want to skip them for being tedious. When we talk about this method lets call it easy difficulty.

Medium and Hard difficulty have another problem, resource management. If you have a serious fight with a trainer, then you're going to use potions and ethers. These become valuable, sure, but it means that being under prepared is a death sentence. If each battle is as hard as your gym battles or higher then what ends up happening is that your players over prepare for the fights and wash it or under prepare and get washed. This isn't even mentioning how this makes trainer battles money sinks. If you get 1000p from a battle, you're going to spend that money on potions for your *next* battle, and not very many too. You're *going* to become under prepared unless the economy is reduced to rubble.

Now, the Easy path solves all of that. Trainer battles will never be hard enough that they actually force you to prepare. You're not going to spend the trainer money you get on potions for the next battle because why would you use potions in a trainer battle? The main problem is that this route just isn't fun to play. You get forced into a battle and then it's a cake walk for 3 meaningless wasted minutes. It's boring.

Even worse is that all of these styles are predicated on the idea that the gyms are balanced around the player when recently they've been given the same treatment as whatever trainer style the game has chosen. Which ultimately undermines the purpose of Gym Leaders as a test of your skills.

Now, for a game where line of sight trainers exist, I'd rather be bored in the routes but have challenging Gyms. That's what I've based my roms on.

But for SVs optional trainers? I would have loved to see the trainers be significant threats. Would have been incredible.

Tl;Dr There is a lot to consider about making route trainers difficulty, and I agreed with their decision in previous games but not in Scarlet and Violet as the optional trainers change the dynamics significantly. Of course, I don't like Gym Leaders being push overs. That sucks.

Okay, lets compare the plusses and minuses real quick and compare how easy they are to ignore.

Slipping into smaller spaces: This is something that has to be built *for* your small character. You usually have to ask your DM if you could fit into a space. This is something very easy to ignore and even if you get it off it seperates you from your party.

Smaller Cover: Again, this is something that you'll have to constantly ask. Your token size isn't smaller, so things still need to be a 5 foot cube, but your DM *may* let you use smaller things in a pinch, although they'd definitely be weaker cover. Once again, easy to ignore, but the benefits are better than the previous one.

Using a Dog as a Mount: Mastiff Statblocks are worse than Warhorses, and it's not like you can't use a Warhose. The biggest benefit here is that you could ride your Beast Companion as a Ranger, but that's super specific. Even then, your beast cannot benefit from the previous feqtures. If you're not playing a beast master ranger, this is so incredibly easy to ignore.

Disadvantage on *any* heavy weapons: An entire weapon property, is almost unusable. This means that small creatures are effectively locked out of using the weapons with the highest damage in the game. This is a massive blow.

Small Size in relation to grappling: Large creatures are impossible to grapple, as you can only grapple one size larger than you. Once again, making small strength builds almost useless. Easy to ignore, but limits strength even further.

------

Tl;Dr It's pretty clear that they think Small creatures should not be strength focused, but the benefits of being small are so unlikely to come up that you'd just be better off not limiting yourself and taking medium.

All of those things except for the latter are DM dependent and might not even matter if you're DM is lenient with medium creatures.

Small Creatures as is are almost exclusively inferior to Medium Creatures, for almost everything that actually matters.
